articles.title_orig: Why China stands to gain from Trump's midterm drubbing
articles.title_zh: Why China stands to gain from Trump's midterm drubbing
articles.content_orig:
You're reading an excerpt from Al-Monitor China-Middle East, where we analyze China's deepening engagement with the region. To get this newsletter in your inbox weekly, sign up here .
WASHINGTON – Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, with Democrats securing at least 54 Senate seats and a projected House majority of between 251 and 268 seats. Upsets in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina underscored the historic nature of the election.
When the new Congress convenes in January, as Elizabeth Hagedorn reports , Trump will confront an opposition empowered to investigate his administration, challenge spending priorities and obstruct his legislative agenda. Much of it will center on the Middle East, the US-Iran war, and business ties and deals with Gulf monarchies forged over the past two years by Trump officials or people in the president’s orbit.
For Beijing, that creates an opportunity. A president facing domestic paralysis may become more invested in securing an agreement abroad, particularly one he can sell as relief for US consumers. Chinese negotiators could conclude that Trump needs a deal more urgently than they do.
The clearest opening concerns Iran. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war for the Republican defeat, while Trump acknowledged that its impact on energy prices contributed to the losses, even as he defended the decision to fight.
The election was not an endorsement of China’s foreign policy, but it gives Beijing political ammunition to argue that negotiations, rather than renewed military escalation, offer the better route out of the conflict and to defend its sustained support for Tehran. Beijing can now portray its diplomatic backing, purchases of Iranian oil and provision of dual-use technology as having helped Iran withstand a war that has exacted a political price from the US president.
China was already expanding its regional diplomacy before the election. This week, as Beatrice Farhat reported , Xi hosted Oman’s sultan, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi held separate talks with senior Iranian and Saudi officials. Beijing also announced plans to dispatch its Middle East envoy to those three countries.
A politically bruised Trump could make that diplomatic pitch more compelling. Beijing can present itself as focused on negotiations, restored shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and economic stability, while Washington wrestles with a stubborn Iranian negotiating team.
Trump will arrive at his meeting with Xi politically weakened at home and under pressure to deliver economic relief. Unlike in previous elections, when he invoked allegations of fraud to challenge the results, Trump was quick to acknowledge the outcome. “I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
The results will make him even more inclined to work with China and avoid an economic breakdown. The trade truce expires in January. Extending it would help avert another round of tariffs, retaliatory measures and uncertainty for businesses. Lowering tariffs could ease import costs, but securing a durable agreement requires China’s cooperation and gives Beijing an opening to demand concessions in return.
That is Xi’s leverage: Trump needs a deal he can sell at home, while China can bargain over its price .
But a weaker Trump does not mean a more accommodating US government. The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could press him to release stalled arms sales to Taiwan, intensify scrutiny of Chinese investments and challenge Beijing over human rights. China may gain leverage with the president only to face a more confrontational Congress on issues it considers especially sensitive.
Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. Read everything they file, from $2/week.

articles.title_orig: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
The head of France's CGT labour union, Sophie Binet (C), said the wave of protests and strikes had reached a new level
More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.
The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.
As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.
The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycÃ©es (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest was reported in several cities.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the RhÃ´ne river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.
The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered  the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.
Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise LÃ©on, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.
A car was set alight during a protest in the centre of Lyon
A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.
Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
Disruption was already reported at schools on Thursday morning
The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of â¬100 a month," Marylise LÃ©on explained.
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".
However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.
The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike on Thursday, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycÃ©es, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.
"Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.
Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.

Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, and the prime minister's residence at HÃ´tel Matignon.
Instead, the march followed another central route from Place de la RÃ©publique to Place de la Nation.
The interior minister had earlier spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

articles.title_orig: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.title_zh: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the reporting threshold in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC on Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data center operators tumbled.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank, which Paraguay's central bank seized amid a solvency crisis, in Asunción, Paraguay, Wednesday. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.
The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.
Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.
Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.
Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. Ted Shaffrey/AP hide caption
As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.
Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.
"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.
Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.
On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.
Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.
Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.
"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.
The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.
Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.
The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Huang is asked to brief Congress on reported Chinese spy relationship
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Huang is asked to brief Congress on reported Chinese spy relationship
articles.content_orig:
Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources.
The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
It instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a Nvidia spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different than his meetings with other executive clients.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.
"Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know."
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. An email to Megaspeed seeking comment was not immediately returned.
The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.
"China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.
The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private . In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.
"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.
Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.
To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.
The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a stand-alone company again.
In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.
Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.
Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.
Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
Hoax bomb threats have caused disruption to at least 25 flights across Europe (latest tally 11:01 ), renewing questions about a possibly coordinated effort to disrupt travel.
At least 32 flights have been disrupted this week in total, with all incidents confirmed to be false alarms.
There is no intelligence yet pointing to any particular group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, amid worries over hybrid incidents targeting Europe ( 15:57 ).
But local reports in Bulgaria and Italy said the emails were signed “the fighters of the Male State,” drawing concerns about possible Russia links ( 18:45 ).
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto described the incidents as fitting the pattern of “warfare below the threshold,” making it difficult to attribute responsibility.
One of the pilots affected by today’s events was being questioned by the French authorities after reportedly declining to land at a military airport ( 17:18 ), with Aer Lingus saying they are “aware of the matter and will of course cooperate with the French authorities.”
Global airlines body Iata has “condemned … attempts to interrupt air transport,” urging the relevant authorities to “find the origins of these hoax threats” ( 16:52 ).
Affected flights accounted only for a tiny fraction of all 27,400 flights were scheduled in Europe today, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol ( 17:24 ).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov, initially as an online community on the social network VKontakte.
Its supporters became known for coordinating harassment campaigns against women, LGBTQ+ people and businesses that had spoken out against discrimination.
In October 2021, the Nizhny Novgorod regional court designated Male State an extremist organisation and banned its activities in Russia.
Pozdnyakov has continued to publish far-right material online and is a prominent supporter of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
On his Telegram channel, Pozdnyakov has neither commented on nor claimed responsibility for the bomb threats.
After reports from Bulgaria ( 17:37 ) and Italy ( 14:38 ) alleging links with the “Fighters of the Male State,” let’s cross to our Russia expert Pjotr Sauer for a quick explanation on the group – with big caveats that we do not really know for sure if they are involved or not.
A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels Charleroi had to inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard lavatory.
The airport confirmed the incident to Belgian newspaper Le Soir and broadcaster RTBF , saying a detailed inspection of all luggage and passengers confirmed no threat.
Here’s a handy map showing some of the affected flights from our visuals department.
The full list of all affected flights today is pinned at the top here.
Two aircraft were inspected at Copenhagen Airport this morning after authorities received emailed threats against them, Danish media reported, without providing details about the flights.
Both planes were later cleared to fly after investigators confirmed there was no threat, according to broadcasters DR and TV2.
A Ryanair flight from London Stansted to Cork airport was also held up on arrival in Ireland this morning after a false bomb threat.
A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian the airport received “an anonymous threat by phone this morning in relation to a specific flight.”
“Elevated additional secutity measures were adopted in conjunction with An Garda Síochána. Nothing of concern was identified and the flight resumed operations with a 90-minute delay. The incident has been fully stood down.”
The airport did not identify the flight, but it was named in Irish media as FR901 from London Stansted, which experienced a delay meeting the airport’s description.
This brings today’s total up to 22 and 30 for this week.
A second LOT Polish Airlines flight – this time LO331 from Warsaw Okęcie to Paris - was also caught up in today’s false bomb alerts.
Following an anonymous report, the plane was forced to stay in Warsaw for additional checks, which showed no reason for concern.
It eventually departed just over four hours late and landed safely in Paris in the early afternoon, the Guardian confirmed.
An email sent to Sofia airport during a series of hoax alerts across Europe today was signed “the fighters of the Male State,” AFP reported.
“We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this forever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red .”
As reported earlier ( 14:38 ), similar messages were also sent to Italian airports.
While 20 false bomb threats across Europe will certainly raise concern, it is worth keeping in mind that this is just a fraction of the overall number of planes flying across the continent every day.
Some 27,400 flights were scheduled in Europe today, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol .
The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux following a bomb threat ( 9:55 , 10:07 , 10:25 ) is being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to media reports in France.
AFP, France24 , Le Figaro and TF1 said that the pilot reportedly insisted on landing at a civilian airport, such as Beauvais or Nantes, prompting the French air force to intercept the plane with fighter jets.
He will now be “questioned under caution,” local public prosecutor Rémi Coutin told AFP.
Aer Lingus has been approached for comment.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

Russian President Vladimir Putin received Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between their two countries, including a pipeline to import Russian gas.
Speaking to journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent much of the day on calls with his counterparts from several Middle Eastern countries, including Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey.
In total, Araghchi held calls with nine different countries in the Middle East. Few details were shared about what was discussed on the calls, simply nodding to "diplomatic efforts to maintain stability in the region."
Notably, Pakistan was one of those countries involved as they have been very closely involved as mediators in U.S.-Iran peace talks. Araghchi spoke to their foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, on Thursday evening.
Araghchi also spoke to Saudi foreign ministers Faisal bin Farhan and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, despite accusations of Iranian involvement in attacks on that country by the Houthi militia in Yemen.
President Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."
"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."
"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis took credit for disrupting travel using a drone at King Fahd International Airport on Thursday.
"We targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam using a drone and our operation caused a disruption of air navigation at the airport," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.
The city of Dammam, which is located in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia, and King Fahd airport have been regular targets for Houthi attacks. Multiple drones have disrupted traffic at the airport this week, according to past announcements.
Two people were killed in a Houthi strike on King Fahd airport on Oct. 22.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its associated strike group will make a port call in Singapore Friday and will not reach the Middle East for at least another two weeks, a U.S. official told CBS News on Thursday.
There are already two carrier strike groups in the region and, which officials say is sufficient firepower to execute any commands issued by President Trump.
Mr. Trump has not signaled yet, in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, whether he intends to order major new strikes on Iran — an option he kept on the table with repeated statements ahead of Tuesday's voting.
The initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit Thursday.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, considered the international standard, rose 2.2% to $96.70, recovering a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before.
Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Thursday in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a message from Iran's supreme leader, according to the Iranian government.
They met amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move on Iran in the wake of U.S. midterm election results that represented a major rebuke of his policies, including, he has admitted, the decision to launch the war with Iran alongside Israel more than eight months ago.
Mr. Trump said repeatedly ahead of the Tuesday vote that he had yet to make a decision on whether to order major new attacks on Iran or to agree a deal to end the war, which Tehran has so far refused to do until the U.S. accepts its core demands to end its naval blockade, ensure a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, and ease sanctions.
During the Rezaei-Putin meeting in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned Russian citizens against all travel to Iran.
"Given the continued risk of a new escalation around Iran, our recommendations to Russian citizens remain unchanged," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters in Moscow. "We recommend temporarily refraining from traveling to that country until the situation is resolved. We also ask our compatriots already in Iran to exercise vigilance and avoid crowds, public events, and areas near military and government facilities."
She said the guidance was "based on the official information disseminated by Tehran," without providing any further detail.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry renewed the regime's rejection on Thursday of longtime and widely held beliefs that Tehran materially supports the Houthi rebels fighting the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen's decade-long civil war. The conflict intensified a couple months ago and quickly became the most active and deadly front in the intertwined conflicts in the Middle East.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the latest accusation of Iranian support for the Houthis, made Monday by European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, "baseless," and said Iran "strongly denied claims that Iranian military experts were present in Yemen."
The U.S. government, along with many other Western nations and the NATO alliance , have demanded for years that Iran stop supporting the Houthis. The support, according to these nations, includes financial backing, weapons and other equipment, and direct coordination and training.

articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has inflicted a dual strike on Vladimir Putinâs Russia, hitting an oil refinery and logistics center within hours using long-range drones.
Reports said the attacks struck Russiaâs third-largest oil refinery and a Wildberries logistics hub in the western Ryazan region, setting both ablaze.
Wildberries processes almost a million orders a day and has been described as a Russian version of Amazon.
âFires broke out at industrial facilities in Ryazan. Power lines were damaged, causing electricity disruptions in parts of the city,â regional Governor Pavel Malkov said .
Ukraine has spent months pummeling Russiaâs oil refineries with drone strikes.
Pictures posted on social media showed large fires at the Ryazan refinery, which can process 17 million metric tons of crude oil a year. Russian independent media outlet Astra said pictures also showed fires at the Wilberries hub, which covers 173,000 square meters.
Malkov said one person was injured in the strikes, and falling drone debris also caused damage.
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Itâs the latest in a wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russian infrastructure that are causing mounting military and domestic woes for the Kremlin.
Earlier in the week, Ukraine said the success of its operation means Russia is being forced to use substandard imported jet fuel for its military planes, causing one to blow up.
On the frontline in Ukraine, the attacks are hampering Russiaâs campaign, which has failed to make significant advances for months amid fuel shortages and heavy manpower losses.
And Russian civilians are also feeling the bite, with inflation spiking and long queues at gas stations throughout the country.
Ukraine says it has knocked out half of Russiaâs refining capacity this year . Itâs launched more than 300 strikes, more than two dozen of which have hit refineries, using sophisticated long-range drones.
Itâs forced Russia, the worldâs third-largest oil producer, to start importing fuel from abroad and halt aviation fuel exports.
The Ryazan facility was also successfully hit on October 15, shutting down one of its processing hubs.
President Donald Trump, before the midterms, attempted to pin the blame on rising U.S. fuel prices caused by his war with Iran on Ukraineâs strikes, and pressured Kyiv to call them off.
Ukraine temporarily halted them but has since has launched a new series of attacks, successfully hitting refineries in Kstovo, Yaroslavl, and the Samara region this week alone.
Russia has responded with brutal missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian civilian targets and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.title_zh: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.content_orig:
An update has ballooned Nier: Automata’s file size to 366GB on Steam.
This is seemingly caused by a bug that has added the full game’s file size to the file size of each DLC. When stacked up, it means you will need 366GB of space to install the full game and its adds-ons, despite it only being around 50GB prior to the update being pushed out.
While initially suspected to be a typo on Steam , RPG Site has since tested this out and indeed found that Nier: Automata now requires 366GB of space. It’s likely the bug will be addressed in a hotfix soon, so it’s worth holding off on installing Nier: Automata or the new update until then. It’s also a handy reminder to switch off auto updates on Steam if you’re unable to revert back right now.
Some report that the issue is fixed on their end, but others are still showing inflated file sizes when they go to install the game or the new update. The store page still says that you just need 50GB of space to install the game. It only seems that you’ll be asked for the additional space when you actually attempt to install it after purchase.
Curiously, the update that caused this hasn’t even added much to the game, instead adding support for three new languages (Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese).
Unsurprisingly, the game is seeing some negative reviews come in, seemingly from those unable to play the game now that it wants to eat up so much space on their PCs. Right now, neither Square Enix nor Platinum Games has acknowledged the mistake, so it’s unclear when a fix will be rolled out everywhere.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
Elon Musk spent at least $445 million in a gambit to help Republicans keep control of Congress, an amount roughly equivalent to someone on a $100,000 annual salary saving every penny for 4,450 years.
To the world’s first trillionaire, it’s a pittance, but the billions of dollars’ worth of business his companies do with the federal government is not. And on Tuesday night, a Republican Party that had embraced Musk lost again and again, ceding control of Congress to a Democratic Party leery of the world’s richest person and keen to put his companies and his work at the White House’s advisory team, which he calls the Department of Government Efficiency, under a microscope.
Nobody may have suffered bigger losses Tuesday than President Trump. But few others had more on the line than Musk, who gambled big and came up holding the midterm’s worst return on investment. Democrats in Congress were already queuing to get their shot at Musk, with possible subpoenas and investigations.
As the bloodiest election for Republicans in recent history wore on, Musk joked on X, the social media site he owns. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he wrote with a shrug emoji.
Musk now faces new threats to his bottom line in places including Texas, where he has based himself and several of his companies. Musk spent at least $5 million to try to reelect Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost. Democrats also secured control of the Texas House and the U.S. Senate, partly by beating Texas Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who effectively benefited from $158 million of Musk’s spending but lost his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.
It was the first statewide win for Democrats in Texas in more than 30 years, and the candidates won in part by hammering Musk, the tax breaks and grants his companies receive, and his relationships with elected Republicans.
“This era of open corruption is going to come to an end,” said Rep. Gene Wu, chairman of the state legislature’s newly empowered Democratic Caucus.
Musk did not respond to messages seeking comment.
Slightly more than half of Texas voters said they had an unfavorable opinion of Musk, according to The AP Voter Poll of more than 5,000 voters in the state. While Musk is overwhelmingly viewed positively by MAGA Republicans, those numbers dip for non-MAGA GOP voters and plummet for independent and Democratic voters.
Those were the voters who Talarico and Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who beat Abbott in the governor’s race, were targeting. The two often framed politics not through partisanship but as billionaires versus everyday Texans, and Musk’s emergence as a major Republican benefactor played into that message.
“Paxton is funded by one dude. Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator,” Talarico told a crowd in his final rally of the election, just after Hinojosa gave a similar excoriation on the same Austin stage.
“We know that Elon Musk got a $1.7 billion property tax break here in Texas, property taxes that the rest of us have to pay full price on,” Hinojosa said.
Even as Musk’s money helped blanket Texas in negative ads largely against Talarico, the Democrats’ message was aimed at the heart of an electorate whose median household income of $85,000 a year is under a pressure test as the prices of gas, groceries, rents and mortgages keep climbing.
Outgoing Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said there was a point where the sheer amount of Musk’s donations became unhelpful to the GOP’s effort.
“You’re reaching the upper bound of the benefit of any of these dollars,” he said in an interview. “People are so turned off by all of the ads, and all you’re doing is running the same ad every single time.”
Musk’s two publicly traded companies, Tesla and SpaceX, both saw prices for their shares drop considerably on Wednesday even as the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index climbed.
Tesla shares declined Wednesday afternoon and wiped out about $40 billion from the electric carmaker’s market capitalization, standing at $1.54 trillion. SpaceX also lost about $40 billion from its market value, now at $1.83 trillion.
Musk lost about $45 billion of his net worth on Wednesday, which stood at $865.6 billion, according to Forbes, though it could rebound.
Investors are signaling some jitters about the impact of the election on Musk’s businesses. Worries that he may face congressional investigations “contributed to the early plunge for his benchmark firms,” said Joe Mazzola, head trading and derivatives strategist at Charles Schwab.
Musk’s genius is also his danger, said Michael Morris, a professor of leadership at Columbia Business School.
“I can understand that the same strategic mind that makes him so good at some of the business ventures and the hedging, it makes him think that he can also take control of politics, but it’s a different animal,” he said.
“He obviously has way more money than he will ever need, and his companies are doing well,” Morris continued. “I do think it’s kind of a game to him.”
Democrats have not forgotten Musk’s time in Washington last year heading DOGE, which blitzed through agencies culling federal workers, and a recent fiasco in which SpaceX internet service in Ukraine, Starlink, was throttled amid the war with Russia.
“Elon Musk waved a chain saw on stage and laughed while he fired public servants and gutted the services Americans rely on,” wrote Rep. James Walkinshaw, a Virginia Democrat, in an X post just before the election. “He must answer for it under oath.”
Back home in Texas, with an incoming Democratic governor, Musk’s dealings with the state, including tax breaks, could face similar scrutiny.
In August, Musk’s companies received a $30 million grant through a state program to build a semiconductor plant that is estimated to create 3,000 jobs, one of several cash infusions he’s received through state programs. And he’s successfully pushed the state legislature to pass laws favorable to his businesses.
Musk has also railed against what he’s called the “woke mind virus,” which appears to be a partisan motivation for him, and shot off a slew of posts on X leading up to the election against Talarico, almost entirely for past stances the Democrat has taken on transgender rights and other progressive causes. That was Paxton’s central attack against Talarico, too, though it fell far short.
“You know you couldn’t pull the wool over their eyes anymore with these culture wars, and they are frustrated with the costs,” said Rep. Christina Morales, a state Democrat from Houston now in the majority in the state’s House.
“We’re not saying you don’t belong here,” she said, but “Texans can’t be bought.” ___
Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.

articles.title_orig: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.title_zh: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.content_orig:
The four-week average of initial applications for unemployment insurance benefits fell to 194,700, the lowest since 1969, according to the Labor Department today. For just the week through Saturday, initial applications for unemployment benefits fell to 189,000, same as in mid-July, and both were the lowest since 1969.
But the population, the labor force, and employment are vastly bigger now than in the 1960s. So these initial applications, historically low in absolute terms, are amazingly low in relative terms.
The four-week average irons out the week-to-week volatility caused by some states missing the reporting deadline, with those weekly claims then falling into the following week. The purple columns indicate recessions, and what happens to initial claims for unemployment benefits before and during recessions.
There have been waves of layoffs at some companies through the left door, while they hired through the right door – big tech has been doing that now since 2022. Overall, private-sector companies have added to their payrolls at a lethargic pace, with some sectors experiencing labor shortages and hiring booms, and other sectors (such as mortgage lending in 2022 and 2023 and some corners of tech) having experienced substantial payroll reductions. Where Are the Jobs? Winners and Losers by Industry .
In addition, the federal government has shed 328,000 workers since January 2025, and state governments (mostly higher education) have shed 53,000 workers since January 2025.
Laid-off staff who receive severance packages, such as continued salaries for x number of months, cannot file for unemployment benefits since they’re still getting paid by their former employer. Many of them find new jobs within the severance period, collect severance plus the salary at the new job, and so they cannot claim unemployment benefits and don’t show up on the unemployment rolls.
But people who could not find a new job within the severance period are eligible to file for unemployment benefits when the severance expires. Their initial applications for unemployment benefits show up here in the data.
Laid-off H-1B visa holders are generally not eligible to file for unemployment insurance benefits and don’t show up in the data here.
What we’re seeing here is that the crackdown on illegal immigration and on abuses of legal immigration rules has changed the labor market by reducing the supply of labor over the past 18 months, and confirms what the separate data in the monthly employment report has also shown from a different angle.
This declining labor force has kept the labor market relatively tight.
Normally , that combination of big job losses at the federal and state governments, and lethargic payroll increases in the private sector, amid a normally growing labor force, would have led to surging claims for unemployment insurance, and by extension surging unemployment rates (data in the jobs report, the next one tomorrow).
The fact that this hasn’t happened shows the impact of the crackdown on illegal immigration which has caused the labor force to decline this year.
Continued weekly claims for unemployment insurance benefits reflect the total number of people who’d initially applied for unemployment insurance at least a week earlier and who still haven’t found a job and are still claiming unemployment benefits.
Continued claims ticked up to 1.72 million in the latest reporting week, with the four-week average at 1.71 million. The only periods since the 1960s when continued claims were lower were some weeks in 2018-2019 and during the labor shortages after Covid.
With initial claims being very low — meaning, the influx into continued claims is very low — rising or falling continued claims suggest the direction of how long it takes overall for laid-off people to get a new job after claiming unemployment insurance.
When it takes longer overall for them to find a new job and they spend more time on the unemployment insurance rolls, these continued claims rise, and they did that coming out of the labor shortages – but remained historically low.
For the past 12 months, the trend has turned the other way, with people spending less time unemployed before they find a new job, and the number of continued claims has declined since late 2025.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers
articles.title_zh: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers
articles.content_orig:
New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.
The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.
The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.
Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact ⁠ (opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.
This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio , covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.
Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
Protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.
Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.
That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.
Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.
Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.
The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

California Pizza Kitchen co-founder Rick Rosenfield told Fox News Digital how two former prosecutors built a pizza empire and how he believes the iconic chain is moving towards a 'new glory.'
Outback Steakhouse parent company Bloomin' Brands is moving to acquire 61 restaurants operated by a major franchisee that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.
Out West Restaurant Group, which operates Outback Steakhouse locations across the western United States, filed for bankruptcy protection in Delaware on Monday, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Bloomin' Brands has entered into an agreement to purchase Out West's assets for approximately $26.3 million, subject to certain adjustments and the assumption of specified liabilities.
MCDONALD'S DEALT LEGAL SETBACK AS JUDGE ALLOWS MCRIB MEAT LAWSUIT TO PROCEED

The company is expected to serve as the "stalking-horse" bidder in the bankruptcy sale process, establishing an initial offer that other potential buyers can seek to exceed. The transaction remains subject to bankruptcy court approval.
Bloomin' Brands also agreed to provide up to $5.5 million in interest-free debtor-in-possession financing to support Out West's operations during the Chapter 11 proceedings, subject to court approval.
Customers enter an Outback Steakhouse restaurant at the Queens Place Mall in the Queens borough of New York, U.S., on Friday, Nov. 9, 2012. (Getty Images)
Out West intends to continue operating its restaurants throughout the bankruptcy process, according to the SEC filing.
Bloomin' Brands said the filing would have no immediate impact on customers, restaurant employees or daily operations at the affected Outback Steakhouse locations.
The bankruptcy involves restaurants operated by the franchisee rather than Bloomin' Brands' corporate-owned locations.

Out West is affiliated with Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, which has operated Outback Steakhouse restaurants across several western states, including California, Arizona, Nevada, Colorado and New Mexico .
The proposed acquisition could bring the franchisee-operated restaurants under Bloomin' Brands' control if the company prevails in the court-supervised sale process.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs buries DEI metrics as it names biggest partner class since 2010
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs buries DEI metrics as it names biggest partner class since 2010
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is burying the diversity metrics of its newest partner class — blaming a changed legal environment as it swells its elite ranks to a 16-year high to fight off defections.
The Wall Street giant led by CEO David Solomon tapped 109 employees on Thursday to join its partnership on Jan. 1, marking the largest promotion cycle since 2010.
As many as 30% of the new class hails from the asset and wealth management division, signaling Goldman’s pivot toward steady fees. A record 13 engineers made partner as the financial giant integrates artificial intelligence across the trading floors.
But in a stark departure from recent years, Goldman refused to provide a racial or gender breakdown of the newly minted rainmakers.
During a background briefing with reporters, executives dodged questions about the missing demographic data, citing the changed legal environment across corporate America.
The comments appeared to be a thinly-veiled reference to the Trump administration’s drive to stamp out so-called Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion policies nationwide.
Internally, bosses have said aiming to build a diverse workforce makes Goldman a better company.
In its previous class announced two years ago, Goldman named 95 new partners. Among them, 27% were women, 6% were Hispanic or Latino and 4% were Black.
The public pivot abruptly ends Goldman’s long-running DEI victory laps and exposes Wall Street’s growing fear of reverse-discrimination lawsuits following the Supreme Court’s crackdown on affirmative action.
While guarding the exact makeup of the 2026 class, the bank disclosed one metric, noting it will cross a milestone of more than 100 female partners out of a total pool of just over 500. Goldman currently employs more than 47,000 worldwide.
Asked by The Post if the supersized class was a desperate maneuver to prevent top earners from jumping to private equity rivals like Apollo and Blackstone, a Goldman executive insisted the partnership hasn’t “lost its luster.”
The bank pointed out that firm revenues have jumped roughly 60% since 2018, keeping the overall percentage of partners at roughly 1% of the workforce.
John Waldron, the chief operating officer and president, was in talks in 2024 to join Marc Rowan’s Apollo, but stayed at 200 West Street after being handed a $80 million stock retention bonus by the board in January 2025.
Waldron is seen as the heir apparent when Solomon finally calls it a day as CEO.
The firm’s newly minted rainmakers can nab yearly salaries north of $1 million, but the staggering wealth of the partnership lies in its secretive, closely guarded bonus pools.
Making the cut grants immediate entry into exclusive, performance-based year-end payout structures that routinely double or triple a partner’s base pay in a good market.
The partner title also unlocks access to Goldman’s proprietary internal investment vehicles, allowing them to personally co-invest their wealth alongside the firm in highly lucrative private equity funds while dodging steep client fees.
Goldman noted 39% of the new class joined as campus hires and 28% started as summer interns.
The incoming partners average 17 years at the bank and hold 20 different citizenships . Sixty-two are based in the Americas, 27 in EMEA, and 20 in the Asia Pacific region .

articles.title_orig: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.title_zh: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Here are the federal income tax brackets for 2027:
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .
